nutshell: Domain-Generalizable person ReID (train on several labeled source domains, test on an unseen one) suffers from a 'domain conflict' problem: methods that only learn domain-invariant features waste useful domain-specific cues, while methods that keep a separate expert per domain can't share knowledge across domains and scale linearly in cost with the number of domains. ACL's CODE-Block instead keeps one shared 'common feature space' per backbone layer: a dynamic branch (several parallel embedding networks combined by per-sample meta-weights from a domain-aware adapter) captures both invariant and specific features jointly, complemented by a static instance-normalization branch, fused via a learned Dynamic-Static Fusion module.
contributions: CODE-Block: replaces the last conv block of each ResNet stage with N parallel embedding networks that all map into the same shared feature space (rather than one dedicated expert network per domain as in prior MoE-based DG-ReID methods), combined via meta-weights from a domain-aware adapter - avoiding the linear per-domain cost of expert-based approaches while still modeling domain-specific variation.

The domain-aware adapter generates its own weight-generator parameters per sample via a 'meta-parameter generator' (a hypernetwork-style module) instead of using a fixed MLP, plus a domain-aware cluster loss that pulls the predicted meta-weight vectors of same-domain samples together and pushes different-domain ones apart.

Dynamic-Static Fusion (DSF) module: normalizes the dynamic-branch and static-branch outputs separately, combines them with a learned per-channel weight vector, and refines the result with SE-style channel attention, rather than naive summation or concatenation.

Large reported gains under leave-one-domain-out evaluation (Protocol-2/3) across Market1501, MSMT17, CUHK02/03, and CUHK-SYSU - the abstract highlights +7.8% mAP / +7.6% rank-1 over the prior SOTA average under Protocol-2 - using a two-stage meta-learning training procedure adapted from MetaBIN.
deficiencies: All four ablation tables (static/dynamic branches, domain-aware adapter, fusion module, embedding stage) show a suspiciously uniform pattern: every added component improves every single metric on every single leave-one-out split with zero exceptions or trade-offs - a very clean result across four separate multi-part ablations, and no variance or multiple-seed reporting is given anywhere to support how reliable these single-run numbers are.

The comparison baselines (SNR*, QAConv50*, M3L*, MetaBIN*) are explicitly the paper's own re-implementations of prior methods under a 'new protocol' (marked with '*'), so the headline SOTA margins are measured against the authors' own re-runs rather than the originally published numbers, with no side-by-side check against those original results to validate the re-implementation.

The paper argues its shared-space design avoids the 'linear increasing costs' of per-domain-expert methods (e.g. RaMoE, MDECL), but never reports parameter counts, FLOPs, or inference latency for either its own method or those baselines - the efficiency argument is asserted, not measured.

Protocol-1 (Table 1) explicitly excludes DukeMTMC for privacy reasons, a reasonable choice, but this means the paper's own headline comparison table isn't directly comparable to earlier DG-ReID papers that include DukeMTMC results, and the brief ethics discussion doesn't connect back to this specific methodological consequence.
notable: The domain-aware cluster loss (Eq. 4) applies a margin/triplet-style intra-/inter-domain loss directly to the network's own generated routing weights (the meta-weights choosing how to combine embedding networks), not to the final ReID feature embedding - regularizing a routing/gating signal by domain identity is a reusable trick distinct from the usual practice of applying metric-learning losses only to the output representation, and could transfer to other dynamic-routing or mixture-of-experts designs. The t-SNE visualization of these meta-weights (Fig. 6) is also a clean, simple sanity check that a learned routing mechanism is behaving as intended (forming per-domain clusters with internal diversity) rather than collapsing to one dominant pattern.
